subject: Canada lost 68,000 jobs. A rate cut still isn't coming.
bodyMarkdown:
If you have a mortgage renewal coming up, or you are a student still hunting for work, Friday's jobs numbers tell you the Bank of Canada is stuck. The economy is shedding jobs while prices keep climbing, which means the rate relief a lot of people have been waiting for probably is not arriving this month.

## What Friday's numbers said

Statistics Canada's **Labour Force Survey**, the monthly household survey that produces Canada's job figures, reported on Friday that the economy lost about 68,000 positions in September, a second straight monthly drop after 42,000 went missing in August. Economists polled by Reuters had expected a gain of 9,200. The unemployment rate rose to 6.5 per cent from 6.4, and the share of adults holding a job slipped to 60.6 per cent. Most of the damage sat in a few places. Educational services together with health care and social assistance gave up 58,400 positions, and manufacturing lost 12,700. Statistics Canada tied part of the education decline to fewer international students, which is a policy choice showing up on payrolls rather than a collapse in demand. Add it up and Canada has lost a net 41,200 jobs in 2026, against a gain of 211,300 over the same stretch last year.

## Why the Bank still may not move

Here is the bind. Inflation ran at 3.0 per cent in August, well above the 2 per cent target, and gasoline did most of that work with a 23 per cent year over year jump while the Middle East conflict dragged on. The picture underneath is calmer. CPI-trim came in at 1.9 per cent and CPI-median at 2.0 per cent, both measures of **core inflation**, which strips out the most volatile prices to show the trend beneath the noise. When the Bank held its rate at 2.25 per cent on September 2, it said upside risks to its inflation forecast had increased, naming the conflict and the shipping disruption at the Strait of Hormuz. A central bank that cuts while headline inflation sits at 3 per cent spends credibility it may want later. An eighth straight hold on October 28 would surprise nobody.

## The part that lands on people my age

The line I keep coming back to is youth employment. People aged 15 to 24 lost 48,000 jobs in September, a second consecutive decline, and the youth unemployment rate held at 13.0 per cent, double the national figure. RBC Economics published a note on Friday saying plainly that the losses were concentrated among young Canadians. I am 16 and in Grade 11 in Richmond Hill, and 13 per cent is the number my friends actually feel. It means the part-time job that used to take two weeks to find now takes most of a season. A weak first job market also tends to follow people for years in the form of lower pay. Women aged 25 to 54 lost 28,000 positions as well, and Quebec, British Columbia and Manitoba drove the provincial declines.

## The takeaway

Between now and the rate decision on October 28, I would watch the September CPI release on October 19 more closely than anything else. If headline inflation cools toward 2.5 per cent, the Bank gets room to look at the job numbers instead of the gas pumps. If it stays near 3 per cent, expect another hold and a Monetary Policy Report that discusses weak hiring without doing much about it. Anyone renewing a mortgage before December should plan around 2.25 per cent rather than a cut, because most bank economists now see the first move waiting until 2027.
